newsitem.title: MAURITANIA: Mauritania has first woman member of parliament.
newsitem.headline: Mauritania has first woman member of parliament.

text.p: The mainly Moslem West African state of Mauritania emerged from its first truly multi-party legislative elections with its first woman member of parliament, provisional results showed on Saturday.
Lalla Zeina Mint Sbaghou, a nurse and mayor standing for the ruling Democratic and Social Republican Party, took 61 percent of the vote in Friday's poll in the eastern constituency of Timbedra.

Elsewhere, provisional results issued by the interior ministry showed ruling party supporters of President Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya heading for victory with at least 32 of the 79 seats in the new national assembly.

The opposition, which boycotted the first such poll in 1992 and denounced fresh irregularities on Friday, had yet to win a seat. It lost seats in two strongholds in the south and in two in the capital Nouakchott.

But relative newcomer, Action for Change, which champions the rights of black Africans and freed slaves in the sparsely populated arid nation straddling Arab and black Africa, made significant advances.
Results showed that at least eight seats will go to an October 18 second round. The ruling party, well placed in many seats for the second round, will contest at least six against Action for Change.
It will contest others against the Union of Democratic Forces-New Era of veteran opposition heavyweight Ahmed Ould Daddah and independents.
The ruling party won 67 of the assembly's 79 seats in the first legislative election in 1992, which the opposition boycotted denouncing irregularities.
Women stood for the first time on Friday, accounting for 26 of the 292 candidates. Mauritania is one of the most conservative and male-dominated societies in west Africa.

Turnout in Nouakchott appeared low with several polling stations reporting less than a third of their electorate voting. Figures from the north, Taya's stronghold, suggested a much higher turnout there.

Opposition supporters, many of whom expressed irritation at the heavy presence of soldiers and other members of the security forces at polling stations, said problems over voting cards prevented many people voting. Some cried fraud.
Poll organisers and officials acknowledged problems with the cards -- mistyped names or identity card numbers -- but officials blamed administrative inadequacies.
Half the 2.2 million people in the poor former French colony at the Atlantic fringe of the Sahara Desert were eligible to vote.
Dominant light-skinned Moors of Arab stock and blacks each make up a third of the population in Mauritania, which won independence in 1960, Arabic-speaking ex-slaves the remainder.
Taya, a French-trained army colonel, seized power in a bloodless coup in 1984. He launched the democratic transition in 1991 and won a six-year term as president a year later.

The opposition was hoping to make its mark on Friday ahead of a presidential election due by January 1998. The Union of Democratic Forces-New Era, Action for Change and the Union for Democracy and Progress are its main flag bearers.
Political pundits say internal rivalries undermined efforts to secure a common opposition stand.
